1778: The appellant company was a private limited company. It had two units, one at Calcutta and another at Calcutta. The second unit was at Calcutta. In the year 1953, the appellant company entered into an agreement with the respondent for the supply of certain goods to the respondent. The respondent paid Rs. 1,00,000 as advance to the appellant company. The appellant company did not pay any further amount to the respondent but on the contrary, it made a default in payment of the instalments due by the respondent. On November 20, 1953, the respondent sent a notice to the appellant stating that the appellant had failed to make the payment within the stipulated period and called upon the appellant to pay the balance of the price within 15 days failing which the respondent would be liable to pay interest at the rate of 12% per annum. The appellant contended that the respondent had committed breach of contract and therefore the appellant could not recover the amounts from the respondent. Held, that the appellant was entitled to recover the amounts under the award from the respondent and the respondent was bound to pay the same to the appellant. The award was made in terms of the agreement between the parties and the appellant was bound to make the payments within the stipulated time. The award being a composite one, it must be construed having regard to the terms of the contract. The award is binding on the parties and cannot be challenged before this Court. The award does not become void or inoperative merely because it contains some terms of its own. It has been held by this Court that the terms of a contract are not necessarily to be found in express terms. The terms of the contracts may be expressed in general language or may be implied from the nature of the contract itself. If the parties have expressly provided so, then the courts will infer no duty to construe the contract as such. But if there is nothing in the contract to show that the parties intended it, then the court will infer no obligation on the part of the parties to do so. In the present case, the respondent had agreed to pay the entire price of the goods supplied by the appellant to it. The appellant had also agreed to pay interest on the said amount at the rate specified in the award. The award therefore became enforceable against the appellant.

The defendant contended that the order was not made under the authority of law but was made under the powers conferred upon him by the Constitution. Held, that the order did not fall within the scope of article 311 (2) of Constitution. It was not merely an administrative act; it was made under authority of law. The order was not a mere formality or a routine act. It was made under powers conferred by the Constitution which were to be exercised subject to certain conditions. The order could not be said to have been made under the power conferred by the constitution. The order did not amount to a decision of a court of law. It was only an administrative act. The order had no legal effect. The order must be regarded as having been made under authority conferred by the statute. The order is not a mere administrative act. It is not a purely administrative act. In the present case, the order was made under a statutory provision. The order being administrative in character, it was not open to the High Court to consider whether the order was one falling within the scope and ambit of article 311 of the Constitution or whether it was made in exercise of its executive power. The order does not fall within article 311(1). The order was made in the exercise of the executive power of the State of Maharashtra. The order therefore fell outside the purview of article 311.
